expert_value.title: Doing More with Less: Innovation Input and Output in Family Firms

decisions.reason: The re-tested claim is Duran et al. (2016), not the individual studies aggregated in either meta-analysis. The introduction, two study methods and Duran reference (AMJ 59, 1224–1264) identify the shipped work. The reference does not print its DOI; support is for the identity, not a claim that the DOI was transcribed from this source.
decisions.context_quote:
To address these issues, Duran,

Kammerlander, van Essen, and Zellweger (2016) published a meta-analytic structural equation

m odel (MASEM) showing that family firms produce more innovation output with less innovation
input. In the present article, we present the results of two empirical studies. Study 1 replicates the

original methodological approach and study 2 provides an extension by using an updated and

enlarged sample of 290 papers, adopting a more advanced multilevel approach, and controlling for

firm age.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: Study 1 reconstructs 92 original primary studies and reproduces the input/output results. Study 2 adds 198 studies; even its original univariate specification retains lower input but loses higher output. The abstract and conclusion explicitly present this agreement and disagreement. These are re-tests of Duran’s contrasts, not merely new age-control outcomes; mixed is supported.
decisions.context_quote:
The results show that while we could successfully replicate the original results of DKEZ

in study 1, study 2 revealed only a weak negative effect of family firm status on innovation input
and no effect on innovation output. Our results suggest that family firms are not producing more

innovation output with less innovation input and that further research should focus on the

heterogeneity within the group of family firms rather than simply comparing family to nonfamily

firms.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: This is a hybrid: Study 1 reconstructs and re-analyses the original meta-analytic sample; Study 2 re-tests the published finding in an enlarged sample of 290 studies. The latter contains 198 additional primary studies, so the record-level replication value has positive different-sample evidence. It should not be understood as all-new individual-level observations.
decisions.context_quote:
Applying these search strategies, we identified 198 additional usable studies. Hence, our

final primary study sample for the extension is 29 0.9

expert_value.title: The acquisition of tense-aspect: Converging evidence from corpora and telicity ratings.

decisions.reason: The original is Wulff et al.’s 2009 tense-aspect paper (Modern Language Journal 93/3, 354–369), explicitly named in the abstract and summarized in section 1.4. Gries & Wulff’s shipped constructions paper is not the finding being tested; Gries’s script and Gries/Stefanowitsch’s collexeme method are analytical tools. The correction identifies a different paper, not a changed report year.
decisions.context_quote:
Prior research has found that the
      frequency and distinctiveness of verb forms in corpora of L1 English production predict L2
      English learners’ tense-aspect production (Wulff et al. 2009). The present study aims to replicate
      these findings and test the predictions of hypotheses of L2 tense-aspect acquisition in another
      group of learners: English-dominant, instructed Spanish learners.

location.expert_location: Abstract, p. 156, lines 10-14 (and References, p. 184, lines 1244-1246)

decisions.label: supported

Results establish the corresponding L1/L2 token-frequency relationship and contingent-frequency pattern. decisions.context_quote:
In our data,
learners mirror the token and contingent frequency of verbs in the L1 corpus, providing
evidence that learning based on the properties of frequency and distinctiveness in L1
Spanish production occurs for the L2 Spanish acquisition of the preterit and the
imperfect. This finding proves that Wulff et al.’s (2009) conclusion for L2 English oral
production generalizes to L2 Spanish writing.

decisions.label: supported

expert_value.title: ‘Mindreading’ Mammals? Attribution of Belief Tasks With Dolphins

decisions.reason: Objection: the expert establishes that 2001 is mentioned, but does not resolve the closest-study rule. The case-study methods specifically say they replicate Tschudin’s follow-up experiments and reconstruct the 2006 protocol; the discussion again calls this a replication of 2006. That report re-tested the same dolphins with added controls and lost significant FBT performance. A joint “2001, 2006” citation and some reused 2001 procedural details do not settle whether 2001 is an independently re-tested original rather than an earlier link. Blind coding lists both; these are not automatically separate originals because year/report differs. Parent must resolve this empirical/report relationship before approving target 0.
decisions.context_quote:
In 2012, our research team initiated an effort to replicate Tschudin’s follow-up experiments. The goal
was to replicate as much of Tschudin’s methodology as could be determined from the summary in his 2006
paper given that the training protocol used to teach the dolphins, the various aspects of the task, and the timeline
it took to prepare the dolphins for the task, were not provided (Table 3). To fill any gaps in Tschudin’s
methodology, we followed the descriptions for the standardized testing procedure presented in Call and
Tomasello (1999), including limiting the number of FBTs presented so as to control for the effect of experience.
decisions.contrary_context_quote:
Tschudin
(2001) reported near perfect performance by four bottlenose dolphins, but upon retesting with additional
controls, the same four dolphins did not perform at levels significantly above chance when their data were
pooled or tested individually (Tschudin, 2006).

decisions.label: objection
decisions.reason: Objection dependent on original identity: failure of the present animal to pass training/FBT is well supported, but the closest explicitly replicated 2006 follow-up also failed significant FBT performance. The title’s “failure to replicate” and comparison with the 2001 positive pilot cannot automatically establish disagreement with 2006. The expert does not reconcile these target-specific outcomes. This is not a recommendation to infer uninformative merely from limitations; it is a request to settle which finding this outcome evaluates.
decisions.context_quote:
After a total of nine months with over 1000 training and probe trials, the dolphin never achieved the
standard criterion set for acceptable performance (Table 3, Figure 1). Despite all of these trials, trying to train
a concept- naïve dolphin resulted in a failure to demonstrate competency at invisible displacement of a fish in
containers and to provide experimental evidence of ToM using the FBT.

decisions.context_quote:
The primary aim of the current study is to extend previous research by examining if

interpersonal synchrony has real world significance in improving children’s helping and empathy

behaviors. This will be done by replicating established tasks conducted by Tunçgenç & Cohen

(2016b), with helping and empathy measurements completed before and after the

expert_value.authors: Sanna S, Pitzalis M, Zoledziewska M, Zara I, Sidore C, Murru R, Whalen MB, Busonero F, Maschio A, Costa G, Melis MC, Deidda F, Poddie F, Morelli L, Farina G, Li Y, Dei M, Lai S, Mulas A, Cuccuru G, Porcu E, Liang L, Zavattari P, Moi L, Deriu E, Urru MF, Bajorek M, Satta MA, Cocco E, Ferrigno P, Sotgiu S, Pugliatti M, Traccis S, Angius A, Melis M, Rosati G, Abecasis GR, Uda M, Marrosu MG, Schlessinger D, Cucca F

decisions.reason: The introduction explicitly identifies the Sardinian CBLB finding as reference 6, Sanna et al. (2010), Nat Genet 42, 495–497; the full author list matches the shipped work. decisions.context_quote:
Recently, a novel association with risk for MS of some

markers within the CBLB gene (Cas-Br-M (murine) ecotropic retroviral transforming sequence b,

3q13.11) was observed in the island population from Sardinia.[6] To assess the associated variant in an

independent sample set from the Italian mainland is cogent for several reasons.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The tested association is the same T allele at rs9657904 and MS risk. Results explicitly report the same direction and comparable effect size in mainland Italy; the abstract concludes further evidence for CBLB association. No-interaction and population-linkage discussion do not contradict that target finding.
decisions.context_quote:
The same allele (T) of rs9657904 SNP, positively associated with MS in Sardinian population, was

significantly associated with MS risk (one tailed p = 7.35 x 10-5 ), and even showed a comparable effect

size (OR = 1.31) also in the Italian mainland (Table 1).

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: Patients and Methods genotype 1,435 cases and 1,466 regionally matched controls from mainland Italy and selectively exclude Sardinian origin. This is positive evidence of an independent population retest, not reuse of the Sardinian GWAS data.
decisions.context_quote:
Background The T allele of rs9657904 within the CBLB gene was recently found to be significantly

associated with multiple sclerosis (MS) in a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in Sardinia.

Objective To replicate this association in an independent population with a different genetic

background. Methods We typed the rs9657904 variant in a sample of 1435 cases and 1466 controls

from the Italian mainland.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The paper defines RS16 as Rubin & Sheremeta (2016) and its reference prints the Management Science citation and DOI. The shipped 2012 SSRN title refers to the same study/report lineage; blind_right is supported as a citation-version correction, not evidence for an additional independent original.
decisions.context_quote: By means of a laboratory experiment, Rubin and Sheremeta (Manag Sci 62(4):985–999, 2016 ), study a bonus-version of the gift-exchange game, including two treatment variations. First they vary whether the effort provided by the agent directly translates into output for the principal, or whether it is distorted by a shock. Second, for the condition with a shock they vary whether the shock is observed by the principal, or not. The authors’ main findings are that (1) the introduction of an unobservable shock significantly reduces welfare; and (2) informing the principal about the size of the shock does not restore gift-exchange. In a replication study we largely reproduce finding (1), but we fail to confirm finding (2).

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The same three treatments were implemented in new 2016 Innsbruck sessions with nine independent matching groups per treatment. Re-analysis of RS16’s adjustment data is an auxiliary explanation of differences, whereas the central attempt is the new participant experiment.
decisions.context_quote: In our replication study, we implement the same three treatments as RS16: In the “No-Shock” treatment, the worker’s effort is not distorted by a shock. In the “Observable-Shock” treatment, the worker’s effort is distorted by a random, zero-mean shock; the principal observes both the effort and the shock before making her decision of how much to reward or punish the worker. The “Unobservable-Shock” treatment is like the Observable-Shock treatment, except that the principal only observes the outcome, which corresponds to the sum of effort plus shock.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly aggregate the two primary comparisons: they reproduce the welfare/effort reduction with unobserved shocks but do not confirm that observed shocks impair gift exchange similarly. Results 1 and 3 and the discussion agree on this partial replication. Hysteresis analyses explain between-study differences rather than replacing the mixed verdict.
decisions.context_quote: We have reproduced RS16’s finding that the introduction of shocks reduces efforts when shocks are unobserved. However, we failed to confirm the result that observable shocks have the same impact on behavior as unobservable shocks.

decisions.reason: The methods and discussion explicitly replicate Experiment 1 of Turri, Buckwalter & Blouw (2015), Knowledge and luck; the full reference prints s13423-014-0683-5. decisions.context_quote: In the present research, we examined the prevalence of Gettier intuitions in counterfeit-object Gettier-type cases by replicating and extending Experiment 1 of Turri et al. (2015).

location.expert_location: Discussion, line 239 (see also Title, line 9, and References, line 374)

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The central Gettier-versus-knowledge null is explicitly rejected, including the original Darrel vignette and the closer first-vignette analysis. Similar effect-size magnitudes do not override the authors’ statement that the null did not replicate and their conclusion contradicting the original claim. The ignorance comparison and ancillary reasonableness checks establish controls, rather than an overall success verdict. Failed is supported for the central finding.
decisions.context_quote: This result did not correspond to that found by Turri et al., who failed to detect a significant difference in knowledge attribution between these two conditions. Notably, the size of the Gettier intuition effect varied by vignette in our research; the Darrel vignette from the original study produced the smallest effect size and was similar to that we calculated using the non-significant result from the Turri et al. Therefore, we do find effect sizes in the same range as Turri et al. when directly comparing like conditions; however, the null result did not replicate.

location.expert_location: Discussion, line 239 (see also lines 241-242 and Conclusion, line 280)

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: This saved version is a completed report with 2019–2021 multinational data collection, analyzed samples and results, despite a registered-report/preprint title and older metadata. It collects independent participant data to re-test the specified experiment; it is neither a prospective plan nor a rerun of Turri’s dataset.
decisions.context_quote: In a large-scale, cross-cultural conceptual replication of Turri and colleagues’ (2015) Experiment 1 (N = 4,724) using a within-participants design and three vignettes across 19 geopolitical regions, we did find evidence for Gettier intuitions; participants were 1.86 times more likely to attribute knowledge to protagonists in standard cases of justified true belief than to protagonists in Gettier-type cases.

expert_value.authors: Cornelissen K. K., Bester A., Cairns P., Tovee M. J. and Cornelissen P. L.
expert_value.title: The influence of personal BMI on body size estimations ans sensitivity to body size change in anorexia spectrum disorders

decisions.reason: The introduction explicitly names [17,18] as the replication and extension, and sample-size design is based on the group-by-BMI interaction in [17], the 2015 Body Image paper with printed DOI. Shipped [20], Visual biases in judging body weight (2016), is a different background contraction-bias study. The second blind target [18] is separately described with a different sample design, not inferred solely from year or DOI.
decisions.context_quote: Statistically, the central finding of Cornelissen et al. [17] that supports a difference in the way healthy controls and women with ANSD perceive body size was a significant interaction between BMI and participant group in predicting self-estimated body size. In this replication study, we followed the same design as Cornelissen et al. [17] by comparing ~100 healthy controls to ~30 women with ANSD, maintaining a sample size ratio of ~ 3:1.

location.expert_location: Materials and methods > Sample size, line 31 (and References, line 170)

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: Agreement on the group-by-BMI interaction and psychological contribution does not settle the whole set. The paper also explicitly tests accelerating overestimation from [17,18]; the full clinical sample has slope near one, and only an AN/OSFED subgroup recovers the original pattern. Authors discuss that difference and leave the exact clinical pattern unresolved. Their replication of the “key finding” refers to the interaction, not an overriding whole-replication success verdict. Mixed is supported.
decisions.context_quote: When analysing the entire clinical group, their self-estimated BMI closely matched their actual BMI, evidenced by a regression slope close to one (see Fig 2), suggesting a relatively accurate perception of own body size across the actual BMI range. However, excluding the participants with a history of bulimia nervosa and repeating the analysis, yielded results more consistent with Cornelissen et al. [17,18], as illustrated in Fig 3. Specifically, the regression slope of estimated BMI on actual BMI had a slope > 1, with accurate estimation at low actual BMI, and systematically increasing overestimation as actual BMI increased. How should we reconcile these differences in the results? We argue that our most important finding is that both multivariate analyses revealed a statistically significant interaction between participant group and actual BMI, irrespective of the inclusion or exclusion of participants with a history of bulimia nervosa.

location.expert_location: Discussion > Participants with a history of ED, line 115

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: New recruitment in 2021–2022 yielded 100 controls and 33 women with eating-disorder histories. The new method-of-adjustment task re-tests the earlier group difference and overestimation pattern, rather than re-analyzing the earlier subjects. Online/in-person and sociocultural-attitude controls are extensions.
decisions.context_quote: In summary, the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18]. We aimed to replicate the differences in perceptual body image identified in these previous studies by improving the design in the following ways: a) ensuring a more accurate alignment of actual BMI ranges across participant groups, b) incorporating measures to control for sociocultural attitudes towards appearance, and c) implementing a refined psychophysical method for body size estimation that avoided emotionally loaded language in the responses.

location.expert_location: Introduction > Emotional significance of deciding “larger/smaller than” another body, line 25

decisions.label: supported

decisions.context_quote:
We previously reported on the success of a psychological intervention implemented to reduce gender
   differences in achievement in an introductory college physics course. In this prior study, we found that the gender gap on
   exams and the FMCE among students who completed two 15-minute self-affirmation writing exercises was significantly
   reduced compared to the gender gap among students who completed neutral writing exercises. In a follow-up study we
   replicated the self-affirmation intervention in a later semester of the same course, with the same instructor. In this paper,
   we report the details and preliminary results of the replication study, where we find similar patterns along exams and
   course grades, but do not observe these patterns along the FMCE.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The abstract’s aggregate verdict and discussion explicitly contrast exam/course-grade agreement with the failure of the FMCE pattern. Exam gender-gap and stereotype interactions are not all significant in this new cohort, but authors describe the exam pattern as similar and the FMCE pattern as different. Mixed follows their account, not a count of significant tests or the original/replication pooled estimates.
decisions.context_quote:
In this prior study, we found that the gender gap on
   exams and the FMCE among students who completed two 15-minute self-affirmation writing exercises was significantly
   reduced compared to the gender gap among students who completed neutral writing exercises. In a follow-up study we
   replicated the self-affirmation intervention in a later semester of the same course, with the same instructor. In this paper,
   we report the details and preliminary results of the replication study, where we find similar patterns along exams and
   course grades, but do not observe these patterns along the FMCE.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The report distinguishes the prior original, an earlier inconclusive attempt, and the present later-semester same-instructor randomized replication (363 included students). “Preliminary” describes its analysis/report status, not absence of empirical results. References 7 and 8 concern the original, not another new cohort to count as a separate original.

expert_value.title: Biology and selection into entrepreneurship: The relevance of prenatal testosterone exposure.

decisions.reason: Bönte et al. (2016) is empirically re-tested in the exploratory entrepreneurial-intent analysis, not merely cited for motivation: the paper describes the original significant right-hand association, specifies a corresponding intent measure, and tests it. Manning’s Klinefelter syndrome study is mechanistic background, with no syndrome sample retest. Nicolaou’s self-employment study is already represented by shipped row 1250 and is distinct from this intent target.
decisions.context_quote: Fourth, in order to replicate Nicolaou et al. (2018), we define the dependent variable, the control variables, and the sample as closely to this study as possible. Our failure to find significant effects does not rule out that 2D:4D is associated with other outcomes related to entrepreneurship such as entrepreneurial intent, as reported by Bönte et al. (2016) for university students; however, it is unclear in how far entrepreneurial intent among students will materialize in actual entrepreneurial behavior later in life. It is also possible that biological factors, including 2D:4D, affect younger persons more than older persons, who have been subject to more intervening nonbiological influences (Bönte et al., 2017). In an additional not preregistered exploratory analysis, we test for an association between 2D:4D and entrepreneurial intent in our data using a measure of entrepreneurial intent similar to one of the measures used by Bönte et al. (2016). We find no statistically significant or suggestive evidence of an association between 2D:4D and entrepreneurial intent in this analysis.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: For Bönte’s reported intent association, the new sample yields no significant or suggestive association, as explicitly described in Results and Discussion. The author cautions that its smaller sample makes the null less informative, but does not declare this attempt unable to test the claim. Nicolaou’s self-employment verdict and the pooled meta-analysis cannot be substituted for this intent outcome. Failed is supported.

expert_value.title: On the limits of language influences on numerical cognition – no inversion effects in three-digit number magnitude processing in adults
expert_value.title_o: On the limits of language influences on numerical cognition – no inversion effects in three-digit number magnitude processing in adults

decisions.reason: The present-study section explicitly names Bahnmueller et al. (2015), using the same stimulus set in comparable German/English samples with reversed instructions. The reference prints the correct title and DOI. Other blind targets Verguts/De Moor and Arend/Henik concern markedness predictions and do not change the identity of the shipped Bahnmueller target.
decisions.context_quote:
In particular, in a conceptual

replication attempt of the study by Bahnmueller et al. (2015), we employed the same three-

digit number comparison paradigm with Arabic digits in a comparable sample of German-

and English-speaking adults. However, instead of asking participants to indicate the larger of

two presented three-digit numbers we asked participants to indicate the smaller of two three-

digit numbers.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: The conclusion explicitly aggregates successful replication of Bahnmueller’s main distance and compatibility findings. The absence of a language-group effect also matches Bahnmueller. Failure of the hypothesized overall reaction-time instruction contrast is attributed to Arend/Henik and Verguts/De Moor, while larger compatibility effects under marked instructions were a new prediction. Neither is an original Bahnmueller contrast that should force mixed for target 0.
decisions.context_quote:
Taken together, we successfully replicated main results reported by Bahnmueller et al.

(2015) showing that distance and compatibility effects in a three-digit number comparison

task generalize across marked and unmarked task instructions. Crucially, however, linguistic

markedness of task instructions did not seem to influence basic numerical processing as the

size of numerical effects was comparable between experiments using a marked compared to

an unmarked task instruction. In particular, results suggest that basic strategies in three-digit

number processing are rather robust against variations of the linguistic markedness of task

instructions.

decisions.label: supported
decisions.reason: Methods explicitly distinguish newly collected pick-smaller participants from re-analyses of the original pick-larger participants. The new sample tests the original numerical effects under a changed instruction; reuse of the original dataset for direct comparison does not make this central attempt solely a reproduction.
decisions.context_quote:
Here we

evaluate distance and compatibility effects in a three-digit number comparison task observed

in Bahnmueller et al. (2015) using a marked task instruction (i.e., ‘pick the smaller number’).

Moreover, we aimed at clarifying whether the markedness of task instruction influences

common numerical effects and especially componential processing as indexed by compatibility

effects. We instructed German- and English-speaking adults (N=52) to indicate the smaller

number in a three-digit number comparison task as opposed to indicating the larger number in

Bahnmueller et al. (2015).
